name: Hume's Guillotine
statement: No set of facts about how the world is can by itself entail how it ought to be.
meaning: Facts about how things are — however many, however well established — do not on their own tell you how things ought to be or what you should do. Somewhere in any argument reaching a moral or prescriptive conclusion, a value has to enter; it cannot be conjured from description alone.
mechanism: A valid deductive argument cannot contain in its conclusion what is wholly absent from its premises. A normative conclusion ('X ought to be done') introduces a new relation, 'ought', not present in purely descriptive premises — so it requires at least one premise that is itself normative. Facts can tell you which action serves a value, but they cannot supply the value.

examples.text: 'Masks reduce transmission, therefore masks ought to be mandated' quietly smuggles in an unstated value ('we ought to minimise transmission', weighed against liberty). The science constrains the means; it does not by itself yield the 'ought'.
'This trait is natural, therefore it is good' jumps from a descriptive claim about origins to an evaluative one with no value premise between them — a textbook illicit move from is to ought.
'People desire pleasure, therefore pleasure is good' moves from a fact about what is wanted to a conclusion about what is valuable, without the value premise that alone could bridge them.

variants.name: The naturalistic fallacy
variants.text: G.E. Moore's related but distinct error (1903): defining 'good' as any natural property. Hume's gap is inferential (you can't derive ought from is); Moore's is definitional (you can't identify good with a natural fact). The two are routinely conflated but are not the same.

variants.name: The fact–value distinction
variants.text: The broader thesis that facts and values are logically separate kinds of claim; Hume's guillotine is its cutting edge.

whyItMatters: It is the standing check against dressing a value judgement as a mere reading of the facts. Whenever an argument slides from what is to what ought to be — in ethics, policy, or science communication — Hume's guillotine says look for the hidden normative premise, because there must be one.

working.text: when an argument moves from facts to a prescription, find the value premise doing the real work — it is always there, stated or not.

working.lead: Keep is and ought on separate lines
working.text: settle what the facts are and what you value as distinct questions; conflating them lets a preference masquerade as a discovery.

working.lead: Use facts to choose means, not ends
working.text: evidence tells you which action best serves a goal; it cannot tell you the goal is worth serving.

limits: It is an influential philosophical principle, not a proven theorem, and it is genuinely contested. John Searle argued in 1964 that from institutional facts — the fact that someone made a promise — one can derive an obligation, since promising builds obligation into its rules (critics reply the norm was hidden in the institution). Ethical naturalists hold that moral facts just are natural facts, dissolving the gap. And whether Hume himself asserted a strict logical prohibition, or a narrower point about moral sentiment, is a live interpretive dispute.
misreadings: It does not say facts are irrelevant to ethics, or that you can never reason your way to an 'ought' — only that you cannot get there from descriptive premises alone, without a value in the mix. Nor is it the same as Moore's naturalistic fallacy, though the two are often blurred.
origin: Stated by David Hume in A Treatise of Human Nature (1739–40), Book III, where he noted that writers on morality slip imperceptibly from propositions joined by 'is' to ones joined by 'ought', a change 'of the last consequence' that is never explained. The name 'Hume's guillotine' is usually attributed to Max Black (1964); the label 'Hume's Law' is associated with R.M. Hare.

sources.text: Hume, D. (1739–40). A Treatise of Human Nature, Book III, Part I, Section I. — the is/ought paragraph.
